```{r}

roc.mle <- roc(data = roctest, predictor = 'probs', response = 'spam.01' )
```

### BIC - LASSO

#### Which are the selected variables?

- Set modify the routines function for logistic regression: 

```{r}
lasso_bic_binomial <- function(y, x, x_test = testdesign) {
  fit <- glmnet(x = x, y = y, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)

  # Use training data to select lambda by BIC
  eta_train <- predict(fit, newx = x, s = fit$lambda, type = "link")
  probs_train <- pmin(pmax(plogis(eta_train), 1e-15), 1 - 1e-15)
  loglik <- colSums(y * log(probs_train) + (1 - y) * log(1 - probs_train))

  n <- length(y)
  n_selected <- colSums(as.matrix(fit$beta) != 0)
  df <- n_selected + 1
  bic <- -2 * loglik + log(n) * df

  best <- which.min(bic)
  lambda_opt <- fit$lambda[best]

  coef <- as.matrix(coef(fit, s = lambda_opt))[, 1]
  names(coef)[names(coef) == "(Intercept)"] <- "Intercept"

  ypred_logodds <- as.numeric(
    predict(fit, newx = x_test, s = lambda_opt, type = "link")
  )
  ypred <- plogis(ypred_logodds)

  output <- list(
    coef = coef,
    ypred = ypred,
    ypred_logodds = ypred_logodds,
    lambda.opt = lambda_opt,
    lambda = data.frame(
      lambda = fit$lambda,
      bic = bic,
      nvars = n_selected),
    fit = fit
  )
  return(output)
}

```



- Fitting the model:

```{r}
biclasso.fit <- lasso_bic_binomial(x = designmat, y = spam$spam.01)

```

- Selected variables:

```{r}
# Coefficients at the lambda with minimum cross-validation error
biclasso.coefs <- biclasso.fit$coef |> as.data.frame() 

biclasso.nonzero <- filter(biclasso.coefs, (biclasso.fit$coef !=0) & (rownames(biclasso.coefs) != "Intercept"))
colnames(biclasso.nonzero) <- 'Estimate'

biclasso.Nvariables <- nrow(biclasso.nonzero)

print(glue("Number of selected predictors:{nrow(biclasso.nonzero)}"))
biclasso.nonzero

```

```{r}

finalperformance <- performance |> rbind(cvlasso.performance[1,], biclasso.performance[1,])
finalperformance$Type <- c('MLE', 'CV - LASSO', 'BIC - LASSO')
```

- A concluding plot: 

```{r}
metric_cols <- names(finalperformance)[1:6]
n_models <- nrow(finalperformance)

plot_data <- data.frame(
  Metric = rep(metric_cols, each = n_models),
  Value = as.numeric(as.matrix(finalperformance[, metric_cols])),
  Model = rep(rownames(finalperformance), times = length(metric_cols)),
  Type = rep(finalperformance$Type, times = length(metric_cols)),
  N_Variables = rep(finalperformance$`N-Variables`, times = length(metric_cols))
)

plot_data$Legend <- paste0(
  plot_data$Type, " (", plot_data$N_Variables, ")"
)

metric_plots <- lapply(metric_cols, function(metric_name) {
  metric_data <- plot_data[plot_data$Metric == metric_name, ]
  upper_limit <- max(metric_data$Value, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.2

  legend_names <- unique(plot_data$Legend)
  model_colors <- c("steelblue", "goldenrod1", "darkred")
  names(model_colors) <- legend_names

  ggplot(metric_data, aes(x = Model, y = Value, fill = Legend)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.65) +
    geom_text(
      aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", Value)),
      vjust = -0.35,
      size = 4
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = model_colors) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, upper_limit),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste("Out-of-sample", metric_name),
      x = NULL,
      y = metric_name,
      fill = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      axis.text.x = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
})

names(metric_plots) <- metric_cols

for (p in metric_plots) {
  print(p)
}

```


## Answer: 

Overall, computed differences in model performance seem nearly negligible. However, if substantial concretion is expected, the BIC approach appears to be the most sensible election when considering all Out-Of-Sample metrics as a whole. For weighted measures like the Log-Loss, however, the Cross-Validated Lasso also arises as a suitable candidate.

It is worth emphasizing, in this sense, that the Specificity-Sensitivity trade-off proposed by the BIC algorithm is more suitable considering the theoretical context of the case. As the BIC reports higher Specificity, it reduces the probability of Type I error occurring (i.e. of non-spam emails incorrectly being labeled as spam). The consequences of a non-spam email being discarded are worse in terms of the user's utility than those of a Type II setting (a spam email appearing in the main inbox). Therefore, Specificity deserves special consideration regarding the final decision for a research paper.

Inference-wise, moreover, model-selection consistency is to be taken into account as a positive trait of the BIC as well. It also entails a non-negligibly more parsimonious equation than the MLE (54 vs 58 variables), while difference with respect to the Cross-Validated Lasso is omittable. When computing confidence intervals and significance tests, however, the MLE estimator behaves much better.

Ultimately, for the aforementioned reasons, the BIC appears to offer an optimal trade-off between all the dimensions analyzed, especially for predictive purposes. Running time for the different algorithms may also help one decide between the three methodologies when dealing with a larger amount of rows (observations) or columns (variables) of the problem's design matrix.




## 8.2.2 Applied Exercise 2

### 8.2.3.1 Data and Context:

```{r}
data(epil, package = "MASS")

# Keep only one row per subject (period 1) to avoid repeated measures
df <- epil %>%
  dplyr::filter(period == 1) %>%
  dplyr::select(y, base)

dim(df)
```


### 8.2.3.2 Train/Test Split and Models



####Question A. Report the average test NLL for: - (i) [intercept-only = 33.28513], - (ii) one-covariate (base) [= 33.28513.]

- Which model is better?

Your answer: The model including base performs better.  



```{r}
set.seed(42)

poisson_nll_vec <- function(y, mu) {
  # vectorized Poisson negative log-likelihood
  # uses lgamma(y+1) for log(y!)
  mu - y * log(mu) + lgamma(y + 1)
}

one_split_eval <- function(df, test_frac = 0.1) {
  n <- nrow(df)
  test_idx <- sample.int(n, size = ceiling(test_frac * n))
  test <- df[test_idx, , drop = FALSE]
  train <- df[-test_idx, , drop = FALSE]

  ###########################
  # COMPLETE THE CODE BELOW #
  ###########################
  
  # Fit models on train
  m0 <-  glm(y~1, family = poisson(), data = train)         # intercept-only
  m1 <- glm(y~base, family = poisson(), data = train)      # with covariate

  # Predict means on test
  mu0_test <- predict(m0, newdata = test, type = 'response')         # intercept-only test set prediction
  mu1_test <- predict(m1, newdata = test, type = 'response')        # with covariate test set prediction

  # Compute mean test NLL
  nll0 <- mean(poisson_nll_vec(y = test$y, mu = mu0_test))              # intercept-only
  nll1 <- mean(poisson_nll_vec(y = test$y, mu = mu1_test))             # with covariate

  list(nll0 = nll0, nll1 = nll1, n_test = nrow(test))
}

res1 <- one_split_eval(df, test_frac = 0.1)
res1
```

###8.2.3.3 Estimating the Expected Out-of-Sample Log-Likelihood Loss


####Question B. Based on the repeated splits: What is the estimated expected average test NLL for each model? Provide the estimate and a standard error.

-Your answer:

```{r}
R <- 1000
out <- replicate(R, {
  tmp <- one_split_eval(df, test_frac = 0.1)
  c(nll0 = tmp$nll0, nll1 = tmp$nll1)
})

out <- t(out) %>% as.data.frame()
colnames(out) <- c("nll0", "nll1")


#We use the sample average and standard deviations as sensible estimators for the true expectation and standard error resquested: 

m0_nll_avg <- mean(out$nll0) 
m0_nll_sd <- sd(out$nll0)/sqrt(R)

m1_nll_avg <- mean(out$nll1) 
m1_nll_sd <- sd(out$nll1)/sqrt(R) 



# Provide an estimate and a standard error for the expected average NLL for each model

print(glue("m0 average : {m0_nll_avg} 
            m0 standard error: {m0_nll_sd} 
            m1 average: {m1_nll_avg} 
            m1 standard error:  {m1_nll_sd}"
))

```

###8.2.3.4 Cross-Validation Check (k-fold)

Question C. Do the CV results agree with the repeated-split results?

-Your answer: Yes, the the model including base reports a much better performance. 

```{r}

kfold_cv <- function(df, k = 10) {
  n <- nrow(df)
  fold_id <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = n))
  res <- lapply(1:k, function(kid) {
    test <- df[fold_id == kid, , drop = FALSE]
    train <- df[fold_id != kid, , drop = FALSE]

    m0 <- glm(y ~ 1, data = train, family = poisson())
    m1 <- glm(y ~ base, data = train, family = poisson())

    mu0_test <- predict(m0, newdata = test, type = "response")
    mu1_test <- predict(m1, newdata = test, type = "response")

    c(
      nll0 = mean(poisson_nll_vec(test$y, mu0_test)),
      nll1 = mean(poisson_nll_vec(test$y, mu1_test))
    )
  })

  mat <- do.call(rbind, res)
  colMeans(mat)
}

set.seed(42)
cv_res <- kfold_cv(df, k = 10)
cv_res
```
